topics.title: Spotting op-amp building blocks
topics.summary: Tell inverting, non-inverting, follower, summing, difference, comparator and integrator circuits apart from how the feedback is wired.

prerequisiteNotes.schem_passive_blocks: An op-amp stage is an op amp with passive blocks around it; the divider and RC patterns reappear in its feedback.
prerequisiteNotes.opamp_inverting: Input through a resistor to the − pin, feedback from output to − pin, + pin grounded: that wiring is the inverting amplifier.
prerequisiteNotes.opamp_noninverting: Input straight to the + pin with a divider from the output back to the − pin is the non-inverting amplifier.
prerequisiteNotes.opamp_comparator: No feedback, or feedback to the + pin, means the op amp is switching rather than amplifying.

lensNotes.circuit: Read an op-amp stage from its feedback: where does the output connect back? To the − input means negative feedback (an amplifier or filter, and V− = V+). To the + input, or nowhere, means a comparator. Then see where the input enters: the − pin (inverting) or the + pin (non-inverting).
lensNotes.signals: The feedback network decides what the stage does to a signal: a resistor ratio sets gain, a capacitor in the feedback makes it frequency dependent (an integrator or active filter), and positive feedback adds hysteresis.

goals: Decide from the feedback path whether an op-amp stage amplifies (output back to the − input) or switches (no feedback, or feedback to the + input)
Tell inverting, non-inverting, follower, summing, difference and integrator stages apart by where the signal enters and what part sits in the feedback
Use V− = V+ to check a stage with negative feedback and find its output from the resistor ratio
Find a comparator's trip point from the reference at its other input
topics.intuition: Read an op-amp stage from its feedback first: output back to the − input means an amplifier that holds V− = V+, feedback to + or none means a comparator that sits at a rail; then where the signal enters and what sits in the feedback say which kind.
topics.why: An op amp multiplies the difference V+ − V− by a gain of 100 000 or more. With nothing feeding the output back, a difference of more than a fraction of a millivolt drives the output to a supply rail: a comparator. Feed the output back to the − input and the loop corrects itself: if the output rises too far, V− rises, the difference shrinks and the output is pulled back. It settles only where V− ≈ V+, so the feedback network, not the op amp, sets the gain. Feed it back to the + input instead and any rise pushes the output further the same way, so it snaps to a rail. There the feedback shifts the + input, so the input must cross back past a second, different threshold to switch it again: hysteresis.
topics.explanation: Each op-amp topic showed one circuit. In a real schematic the op amp is a triangle with parts around it, and you have to name the stage before you can use its formula. Ask three questions in order. First, where does the output connect back? To the − input: negative feedback, an amplifier or filter, and V− = V+. To the + input, or nowhere: a comparator, its output at one rail or the other; feedback to + adds hysteresis and makes a Schmitt trigger. Second, where does the signal enter? Through a resistor to the − pin, with + held at a fixed voltage: inverting, gain −Rf/Rin. Several input resistors into that pin make a summing amplifier. Straight into the + pin: non-inverting, gain 1 + Rf/Rg, and with the output wired straight back to − it is the follower, gain 1. Signals at both pins through matched resistor pairs: a difference amplifier. Third, what is in the feedback? A resistor gives a fixed gain. A capacitor makes the gain depend on frequency: an inverting stage with a capacitor from output to − is an integrator. The passive blocks reappear too: Rf and Rg form a divider from the output.

workedExample.problem: A light detector runs from a single 5 V supply (assume rail-to-rail op amps). A sensor stage gives 0.5 V at node s. Op amp X1: s goes straight to its + pin; Rf = 22 kΩ runs from its output (node b) to its − pin, and Rg = 10 kΩ from the − pin to ground. Op amp X2: its + pin connects to b; its − pin sits on node ref, between R3 = 10 kΩ (to 5 V) and R4 = 10 kΩ (to ground); its output drives an LED through a resistor and connects to nothing else. Name each stage, find V_b, and find the voltage at s that turns the LED on.
steps: X1's feedback: its output returns to its − pin through Rf. That is negative feedback, so X1 is an amplifier and holds V− = V+.
X1's input: the signal enters at +, and Rf–Rg is a divider from the output back to −: a non-inverting amplifier with G = 1 + Rf/Rg = 1 + 22 kΩ / 10 kΩ = 3.2.
V_b = 3.2 × 0.5 V = 1.6 V. Check with V− = V+: the Rf–Rg divider hands back 1.6 V × 10 kΩ / (22 kΩ + 10 kΩ) = 0.5 V to the − pin, equal to V+.
X2's feedback: its output goes only to the LED, with nothing back to either input. X2 is a comparator: its output sits at 5 V when V+ > V−, and at 0 V otherwise.
X2's reference: R3 and R4 divide the supply, V_ref = 5 V × 10 kΩ / (10 kΩ + 10 kΩ) = 2.5 V on the − pin. Now V_b = 1.6 V is below 2.5 V, so X2's output is at 0 V and the LED is off.
Trip point: the LED turns on when V_b passes 2.5 V, that is when V_s passes 2.5 V / 3.2 = 0.781 V.
Both stages use the same triangle. Only where the output connects back made X1 an amplifier and X2 a switch.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "The \"operational\" amplifier"
sources.note: Checked that an op amp's open-loop gain is so high (hundreds of thousands) that microvolts of input difference saturate it, and that with no feedback it acts as a comparator whose output sits at one extreme or the other.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Divided feedback"
sources.note: Checked that negative feedback holds the two inputs at practically the same voltage, the non-inverting gain 1 + R2/R1, the inverting gain −R2/R1, and that the follower is the gain-of-1 limit.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Positive feedback"
sources.note: Checked that feedback to the + input drives the output to saturation and latches it, and that a feedback resistor to + gives a comparator two switching thresholds (hysteresis).

templates.prompt: Read this op-amp stage (±12 V supplies, not drawn) from its wiring: where does the output connect back to, and where does the signal enter? What is this circuit?

choices.text: A comparator with hysteresis (a Schmitt trigger)
choices.feedback: Right: the output returns to the + input, so the feedback is positive. The output snaps to a rail, and R2 shifts the switching point depending on which rail it is at.

choices.text: A non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 1 + R2/R1
choices.feedback: A non-inverting amplifier feeds a fraction of the output back to the − input (with a leg from − to ground), and the signal goes straight to +. Here the feedback lands on +, and the − input is simply grounded.

choices.text: An inverting amplifier with a gain of −R2/R1
choices.feedback: This looks like the inverting layout, but check the pins: an inverting amplifier needs R1 and R2 to meet at the − input, with + grounded. Here they meet at +, and − is grounded, which turns negative feedback into positive feedback.

choices.text: A plain comparator with no hysteresis
choices.feedback: A plain comparator has no feedback at all: just the signal on one input and a reference on the other. R2 carries part of the output back to the input, which moves the threshold after each switch; that is hysteresis.

templates.explanation: Read an op-amp stage in two steps. First, where does the feedback go? Here R2 runs from the output to the + input: positive feedback, so this is a comparator, not an amplifier. Second, where does the signal enter? Through R1 to the same + input, with − at 0 V. That is a non-inverting Schmitt trigger: it switches high when the signal rises past about +1.2 V and low when it falls past about −1.2 V (the rail × R1/R2). That gap is the hysteresis, and it stops noise making it chatter.
hints: Follow the wire from the output back to an input. Which pin does it reach, + or −?
Feedback to the − input makes an amplifier; feedback to the + input makes a switch.

followUps.prompt: Why can't this circuit settle with its two inputs at the same voltage, the way an amplifier does?

choices.text: Feedback to the + input makes any small input difference grow until the output hits a rail
choices.feedback: Right: if the output rises a little, R2 lifts the + input, which makes the output rise even more. The only stable places are the rails.

choices.text: The op amp has no supply drawn in this circuit, so it can't hold any middle voltage
choices.feedback: The op amp is powered as usual (the supply pins just aren't drawn). The wiring, not the supply, makes it switch.

choices.text: R2 is too large for an amplifier; with R2 smaller than R1 the stage would settle
choices.feedback: Changing R2 only changes how wide the hysteresis is. Any feedback to the + input is positive feedback, whatever its size.

choices.text: The − input is grounded, and an op amp with a grounded input always acts as a comparator
choices.feedback: The inverting amplifier grounds its + input and is still an amplifier. What matters is which input the feedback reaches.

followUps.explanation: An op amp amplifies V+ − V− by around 100 000. With feedback to the − input, a rise in the output raises V− and shrinks the difference, so the loop settles where V− = V+. With feedback to the + input, a rise in the output raises V+ and grows the difference, so the output runs away to a rail and stays there until the signal drags it back past the threshold.

templates.prompt: What kind of op-amp stage is this? Look at which input the output returns to, and what part it returns through.

choices.text: An inverting integrator
choices.feedback: Right: negative feedback through a capacitor. The − input is a virtual ground, so a steady input pushes a steady current Vin/R1 into C1, and the output ramps.

choices.text: A differentiator
choices.feedback: A differentiator swaps the two parts: the capacitor in series with the input, and a resistor in the feedback. Here the capacitor is in the feedback path.

choices.text: An inverting amplifier with a fixed gain
choices.feedback: A fixed gain needs a resistor in the feedback, so the gain is the ratio −Rf/R1. A capacitor's impedance changes with frequency, so the gain here does too.

choices.text: A comparator
choices.feedback: A comparator has no feedback, or feedback to the + input. C1 connects the output to the − input, which is negative feedback: the op amp is working in its linear region.

templates.explanation: Feedback goes from the output to the − input, and the signal enters through R1 to that same − input, with + grounded: this is the inverting layout. The feedback part is a capacitor instead of a resistor, so it is an integrator. Its gain magnitude, 1/(2πf·R1·C1), is large at low frequencies and falls as frequency rises. (An active low-pass filter is the same circuit with a resistor across C1 to limit the low-frequency gain.)
hints: Start with the pins: which input does the feedback reach, and which does the signal reach?
Now ask what a capacitor in the feedback does that a resistor wouldn't.

followUps.prompt: A steady positive voltage is applied at the input. Why does the output ramp steadily downward instead of settling?

choices.text: The − input stays at 0 V, so a steady Vin/R1 flows into C1, ramping C1's voltage, and so the output, steadily
choices.feedback: Right: a constant current into a capacitor makes its voltage change at a constant rate (dV/dt = I/C). The output ramps until it reaches a rail.

choices.text: The capacitor slowly charges up to the input voltage through R1, and after that the output stops moving
choices.feedback: That is a plain RC circuit charging from a source. Here the − input is a virtual ground, so the current Vin/R1 never falls; nothing stops the ramp except the supply rail.

choices.text: The op amp oscillates, because a capacitor in its feedback path makes the whole loop unstable
choices.feedback: A capacitor from output to the − input is negative feedback and perfectly stable; it is the classic integrator.

choices.text: Current flows out of the − input into the op amp itself, so it steadily discharges the capacitor C1
choices.feedback: An ideal op amp's inputs draw no current. All of R1's current goes into C1.

followUps.explanation: The negative feedback keeps V− = V+ = 0 V. So the current through R1 is Vin/R1, and it must flow on into C1. A steady current into a capacitor changes its voltage at the steady rate I/C, and since one side of C1 is held at 0 V, the output moves by that amount: Vout falls at Vin/(R1·C1) volts per second.

schematic.netlist:
Integrator
VS in 0 SIN(0 1 1k)
R1 in inv 10k
C1 inv out 10n
X1 0 inv out OA
.model OA OPAMP(A=1e5)

templates.prompt: Two signals, V1 and V2, feed this op-amp stage. What does it do?

choices.text: It amplifies the difference: Vout = (47k/10k)·(V2 − V1)
choices.feedback: Right: V1 enters at the − input (through R1, with R2 as feedback) and V2 at the + input (through the R3–R4 divider). With matched ratios, only V2 − V1 is amplified.

choices.text: It adds them with gain: Vout = −(47k/10k)·(V1 + V2)
choices.feedback: A summing amplifier brings every input to the − input through its own resistor, with + grounded. Here V2 goes to the + input, so it is treated with the opposite sign to V1: subtracted, not added.

choices.text: It amplifies V2 only, and V1 just sets a fixed DC bias
choices.feedback: V1 reaches the − input through R1 and pushes current into the feedback resistor R2, so it moves the output as much as V2 does, in the opposite direction.

choices.text: It compares them and switches the output to a rail
choices.feedback: A comparator has no negative feedback. R2 runs from the output to the − input, so this op amp works in its linear region and V− = V+.

templates.explanation: Read it pin by pin. The feedback R2 goes to the − input: negative feedback, an amplifier. V1 enters the − input through R1: that half is an inverting amplifier (gain −R2/R1). V2 enters the + input through the R3–R4 divider: that half is non-inverting. With R4/R3 = R2/R1, the two gains are equal and opposite, so Vout = (R2/R1)(V2 − V1) = 4.7 × (V2 − V1).
hints: Find which pin each input reaches.
An input on the − pin is inverted; an input on the + pin is not.

followUps.prompt: Why does R4/R3 have to match R2/R1?

choices.text: So a voltage common to both inputs cancels and only the difference is amplified
choices.feedback: Right: if V1 and V2 rise together, a mismatch would let part of that common rise through to the output.

choices.text: So the two inputs draw the same current and load their two sources equally
choices.feedback: They don't: V1 sees R1 into a point that follows V2, while V2 sees R3 + R4. Input currents differ even when the ratios match.

choices.text: So the gain from the difference to the output comes out at exactly 1
choices.feedback: The gain here is 4.7. Matching sets which part is amplified (the difference), not how much.

choices.text: It doesn't matter, because the op amp's negative feedback corrects any mismatch
choices.feedback: The op amp only makes V− = V+. The resistors decide what that means for the output; a mismatch lets common-mode voltage leak through.

followUps.explanation: The − side amplifies V1 by −R2/R1. The + side divides V2 by R4/(R3 + R4) and then amplifies it by 1 + R2/R1. These two gains are equal and opposite only when R4/R3 = R2/R1, and then a voltage applied to both inputs at once cancels exactly.

V2 b 0 1.5
R1 a inv 10k
RF inv out 47k
R3 b p 10k
R4 p 0 47k
X1 p inv out OA

templates.prompt: A sensor with 10 kΩ of its own resistance drives a 1 kΩ load through this op-amp stage. Read the wiring: what is the stage?

choices.text: A voltage follower (buffer) with a gain of 1
choices.feedback: Right: all of the output returns to the − input, so the op amp makes Vout = V− = V+ = the sensor voltage.

choices.text: A short circuit: the output is joined to the input, so the op amp fights the sensor
choices.feedback: The output is joined to the − input, not to the signal. The − input draws no current, so nothing is shorted; the op amp simply drives its output until it matches the + input.

choices.text: An inverting amplifier with a gain of −1
choices.feedback: An inverting amplifier needs the signal to enter the − input through a resistor, with + grounded. Here the signal goes to +, so the output is not inverted.

choices.text: A comparator, because there is no feedback resistor
choices.feedback: Feedback doesn't need a resistor. The wire from output to − input is the strongest negative feedback there is: it returns the whole output.

templates.explanation: The whole output returns to the − input: negative feedback with nothing in the way, so the gain is 1 + 0/Rg = 1. The signal enters at +. This is the voltage follower. It copies the sensor's voltage but draws no current from it, and drives the 1 kΩ load from its own supply. Connected directly, the load would have divided the sensor's voltage down to 1/11.
hints: Where does the signal enter, and where does the output return?
A non-inverting amplifier with Rf = 0 has what gain?

templates.prompt: This non-inverting amplifier (ideal op amp, ±12 V supplies) has Rf = {Rf} and Rg = {Rg}, and its input is {Vin}. Rf is doubled to {new_Rf} (a second {Rf} added in series). What happens to the output voltage?

feedback.down: A bigger Rf does hand back a smaller fraction of the output to the − input. But the op amp doesn't stop there: it keeps moving its output until that smaller fraction of it again equals {Vin}.
feedback.same: Rf is part of the feedback divider, so it sets the gain. The op amp drives its output to whatever value makes the divider return exactly {Vin} to the − input, and Rf changes the fraction the divider returns.

whatIf.factorHint: The gain is 1 + Rf/Rg, and only the Rf/Rg part depends on Rf: work out the gain before and after.

templates.explanation: The gain is 1 + Rf/Rg. Doubling Rf doubles only the Rf/Rg part: the gain goes from 1 + {Rf}/{Rg} to 1 + {new_Rf}/{Rg}, and the output from {before} to {after}. That is ×{ratio}, less than double, because the "1" does not change.
hints: Write the gain as 1 + Rf/Rg. Which part changes?

followUps.prompt: Rf doubled, but the output did not double. Why?

choices.text: The gain is 1 + Rf/Rg: only the Rf/Rg part doubles, and the 1 (the input itself, which the output always contains) stays the same
choices.feedback: Right: the output is V− plus the drop across Rf. V− stays at Vin; only the drop across Rf doubles.

choices.text: Doubling Rf halves the current through it, which cancels part of the change
choices.feedback: The current through Rf doesn't change: it is Vin/Rg, set by Rg with V− held at Vin. The same current through twice the resistance gives twice the drop across Rf.

choices.text: The output is limited by the supply rails
choices.feedback: These outputs are a few volts, far from the rails. The shortfall comes from the gain formula itself.

choices.text: The op amp's own gain is too low to follow the change
choices.feedback: The open-loop gain is around 100 000; the feedback network alone sets the result.

followUps.explanation: With negative feedback, V− = Vin, so the current through Rg is Vin/Rg. That current also flows through Rf, so Vout = Vin + (Vin/Rg)·Rf. Doubling Rf doubles only the second term. The gain gets close to doubling only when Rf is much bigger than Rg.

templates.prompt: In this non-inverting amplifier (±12 V supplies, not drawn; input {Vin}, Rf = {Rf}, Rg = {Rg}), Rf is doubled to {new_Rf} (a second {Rf} added in series). The output rises. What happens to the voltage at the op amp's − input?

feedback.up: The output does rise, but with the bigger Rf the divider hands back a smaller fraction of it. The op amp only moves its output while V− and V+ differ, and V+ is still {Vin}.
feedback.down: For an instant the bigger Rf does pull the − input down. But the op amp sees V− below V+ and raises its output, and it keeps raising it for as long as V− stays below V+.

templates.explanation: The feedback goes to the − input, so it is negative feedback: the op amp drives its output to whatever value makes V− equal V+. V+ is the input, {Vin}, so V− stays at {Vin} whatever Rf is. Changing Rf changes how much output it takes to get there, which is the gain.
hints: Which input does the feedback reach? What does negative feedback do to the two inputs?

followUps.prompt: Why does the − input stay at {Vin}?

choices.text: The op amp amplifies V+ − V− enormously, and because the feedback returns to −, the output always moves to shrink that difference; it settles only when V− = V+
choices.feedback: Right: this is what "feedback to the − pin means V− = V+" is. Any difference of more than tens of microvolts would drive the output hard toward closing it.

choices.text: Current from the input flows through the op amp from the + input to the − input
choices.feedback: The inputs draw no current and aren't connected to each other inside. V− gets its voltage from the output through Rf, not from V+.

choices.text: Rg fixes the voltage at the − input
choices.feedback: Rg has no voltage source of its own; V− is only above 0 V because the output drives current through Rf into Rg. The op amp picks the output that makes that voltage equal Vin.

choices.text: Any feedback does this; it would work the same with the feedback to the + input
choices.feedback: Feedback to the + input is positive: it grows the difference instead of shrinking it, and the output snaps to a rail (a comparator).

followUps.explanation: An op amp's output is A·(V+ − V−) with A around 100 000. With feedback to the − input, a rise in the output raises V−, which reduces V+ − V−, which pulls the output back. The loop settles where V+ − V− = Vout/A, tens of microvolts at most: in practice V− = V+.

templates.prompt: This non-inverting amplifier runs from ±12 V supplies (not drawn). With Rf = {Rf}, Rg = {Rg} and {Vin} in, the output should be {h0}. The meter readings are below. Which fault explains them?

faults.text: Rf is open (cracked, or a dry joint)
faults.feedback: With Rf open nothing brings the output back: Rg would hold the − input at 0 V, the op amp would drive its output to near the +12 V rail, and Rf would carry no current.
faults.why: The − input reads 0 V instead of {Vin}, so the feedback loop is broken, and no current flows in Rf. With V+ above V− and no feedback, the op amp drives its output to near the +12 V rail.

faults.feedback: With Rg open no current could flow through Rf, so it would drop nothing: the − input would equal the output, and the stage would become a follower with output = input and 0 A in Rf.
faults.why: The output equals the input and the − input equals both, so the loop works but the gain is 1. No current flows in Rf, so there is no drop across it: the leg to ground (Rg) is missing.

faults.text: Rf is shorted (a solder bridge across it)
faults.feedback: With Rf shorted the output would connect straight to the − input, so the stage would become a follower (output = input), while the normal current, Vin/Rg, still flowed through the bridge where Rf is.
faults.why: The output equals the input, so the gain has become 1, yet the normal current Vin/Rg still flows where Rf is. So the Rf position still conducts but drops no voltage: it is bridged.

faults.feedback: With Rg shorted the − input would be tied to 0 V, so the op amp could never make V− equal V+: the output would go to near the +12 V rail and push 12 V/Rf through Rf into the short.
faults.why: The − input reads 0 V even though a large current flows in Rf: the output is pushing current through Rf into a dead short to ground. The op amp can't pull V− up to {Vin}, so its output sits near the +12 V rail.

templates.explanation: Read the readings the way you read the drawing. In a working stage the feedback makes V− = V+. If V− has fallen to 0 V, the loop is broken and the output sits at a rail; the current in Rf then tells you whether Rf is open (no current) or Rg is shorted (a large current). If the output only equals the input, the stage has become a follower; the current in Rf tells you whether Rg is missing (no current) or Rf is bridged (normal current).
hints: First check the − input: is it still equal to the input? If not, the feedback loop is broken.
Then use the current in Rf to tell the two possibilities apart.

templates.prompt: The op amp runs from ±12 V supplies (not drawn). The input is a steady {Vin}, R1 = {Rin} and R2 = {Rf}. Find the output voltage (with its sign).
templates.explanation: R2 runs from the output to the − input: negative feedback, so V− = V+. The signal enters the − input through R1 and the + input is grounded: an inverting amplifier. V− is held at 0 V, so R1 carries {Vin}/{Rin}; that current can't enter the op amp, so it flows on through R2, and the output must sit below 0 V by that current times R2. Vout = −({Vin} × {Rf}/{Rin}) = {answer}, inside the ±12 V rails.
hints: Which input does the feedback reach, and which input does the signal reach?

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the sign is not. The signal enters the − input, so the output moves the opposite way: a positive input gives a negative output.
That is the non-inverting gain, 1 + R2/R1. It applies when the signal goes to the + input. Here the signal goes through R1 to the − input and + is grounded, so the gain is −R2/R1.
The ratio is upside down. The current set by R1 flows through R2, so the output is that current times R2: the gain is −R2/R1, not −R1/R2.
